newsitem.title: INDIA: India's main opposition party slams "half budget".
newsitem.headline: India's main opposition party slams "half budget".

text.p: The Indian parliament on Friday began a crucial debate on the annual budget unveiled last month with the main opposition party saying the euphoria it had generated would be shortlived.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram presented the budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) on February 28. The lower house of parliament is expected to vote on it later this month.
"It is, in fact, a half budget," former prime minister Atal Behari Vajpayee said, opening the debate for his rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Vajpayee was referring to a yawning oil subsidy deficit that Chidambaram did not take into account in the budget, otherwise hailed by business as a bold and innovative package.

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front coalition says the estimated 155 billion-rupee ($4.3 billion) oil pool account deficit -- the money the government owes its state-run companies for oil imports -- will be addressed later.

Vajpayee said an imminent increase in the prices of petroleum products, a heavily subsidised commodity, would have a cascading effect on the prices of essential commodities. "What has been seen so far is the rose," he said. "But the real effect will be known when its thorns start pricking."
"When the government effects the hike in the prices of petroleum products to tackle the deficit, the already thinning euphoria over the budget would totally vanish," he said.

Vajpayee's criticism of Chidambaram's tax proposals, which substantially reduced both corporate and individual taxes, came close to the views of the Congress party which reluctantly shores up Deve Gowda's nine-month old minority government in parliament.
Like the BJP, the Congress too has described the tax proposals as pro-rich.
The United News of India (UNI) quoted a Congress official as saying the party could block the budget if the government did not increase its allocation for poverty alleviation and agriculture.
"The Congress is now pressuring the government to budge on their demand," UNI quoted H. Hanumanthappa as telling reporters after the Congress Parliamentary Party met earlier on Friday.
The United Front has fewer than 200 deputies in the lower house of parliament, leaning on the Congress, with some 140 lawmakers, to fend off an incessant challenge from the BJP.
Political analysts said the Congress was unlikely to carry out its threat to block the government's budget because it was not in a position to gain from the snap polls that would follow.
